Both plans end the old-growth beech, a grievous failure of stewardship. Yet plan 2 preserves the valley dialect, a living cultural heritage, while sacrificing the ski club; I judge that the greater human good.
Plan 1 preserves more of creation’s fabric—hill village, honey producers, and shared livelihoods—while both plans sadly end the salmon run. Stewardship favors plan 1.

Plan 1 sustains two living community traditions—the harvest festival and folk dance group—that bind neighbours and generations; the puppet theatre, though worthwhile, is a narrower loss. Both plans sadly end the minority-language radio.
Plan 2 preserves the folk dance group as well as the newspaper, archive and puppet theatre. Since what ends is gone for good, keeping more communal life is better stewardship.
Creation's irreplaceable old-growth beech and the valley's living dialect and summer pasture weigh more than recreation and a local lynx population; we are stewards, not owners.
Plan 1 keeps more communal and minority-language life; losing the radio station harms a vulnerable voice, while the puppet theatre alone does not outweigh the festival, dance group, and radio.
Plan 1 is better: it spares the only lichen of its kind and a pilgrimage path; a unique extinction is a grave breach of stewardship, though losing the village and salmon is grievous.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the folk dance group; both lose the minority-language radio and harvest festival, so Plan 2 better serves community and cultural care.
Plan 1 spares the honey producers while both plans lose the village and salmon; it is stewardly to avoid needless additional loss of creation and livelihood.
Plan 2 is better: it preserves more of the community’s shared life—harvest festival and folk dance—while the minority-language radio loss is the same under both. Fewer closures serve our neighbor.
Plan 1 better: preserving the honey producers' association supports pollinators and small rural livelihoods, a form of creation care; losing a rafting company is regrettable but less foundational.

Both plans lose the harvest festival and minority-language radio; the only difference is puppet theatre versus folk dance group. I see no pastoral warrant to rank one cultural good above the other, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 better sustains vulnerable minority-language neighbors and living rural community traditions; the others are valuable but more institutional.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does and also keeps the evening school for adults, a good for neighbors and lifelong learning. With all else equal, that additional good makes Plan 1 better.
Plan 2 preserves more community goods—adult education, music, science, and creation care—while sacrificing one academic department. Stewardship favors fewer irreversible losses.
Both plans irreversibly end three real goods; Scripture gives no calculus to rank frogs, festival, credit union, mangoes, buffalo, and terraces. I would grieve either and cannot call one better.

Plan 1 keeps more of creation's entrusted goods and community life: seed bank, botanical garden, evening school, observatory and classics. Only the student orchestra ends, so it is the better stewardship.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony, part of God’s creation entrusted to our care. The other losses are identical, so stewardship favors keeping more life.
Plan 1 better keeps the adult evening school, a practical work of neighbor-love and lifelong learning; both plans safeguard the seed bank and botanical garden, so creation care is equal.
Plan 1 better: it keeps the owl colony and family mill, honoring creation and household livelihood; losing the union and coop is a real cost, but not enough to outweigh.

Plan 1 preserves more of the six, including adult education and the botanical garden; it ends only orchestra and observatory, while plan 2 also closes the evening school. Stewardship favors keeping what can continue.

Both keep the seed bank and botanical garden, which I weigh heavily as care for creation. Plan 2 also keeps the evening school and observatory, serving neighbors and wonder, while losing only classics besides the orchestra.

Stewardship of God’s creation weighs heavily: the seed bank and botanical garden preserve biodiversity for future generations and cannot be restored once lost. Losing the evening school is a real cost, but plan 1 better keeps our entrusted care.
Plan 1 preserves more of the town’s common life and the barn owl colony; as stewards of creation we should avoid needless loss.
Plan 1 keeps the corner shop as well as the storks, post office, and craft circle; plan 2 loses the shop, while both lose the bus and fire brigade. So plan 1 is better.

Stewardship of creation and love of neighbor favor preserving more of the town's life and livelihood. Plan 2 keeps the owl colony, textile mill, union, brewery, and band; the bicycle cooperative ends either way.
Plan 2 better honors our stewardship of God’s creation by preserving the barn owl colony, and it sustains the family mill and repair cooperative—local callings that serve community life.
Plan 2 keeps the shop and bus that sustain rural neighbours and preserves more services; losing the storks is a real grief, but the fire brigade ends either way.

Both plans irrevocably lose the textile mill and bicycle cooperative; the remaining choice between a workers’ union and an owl colony pits human community against creation, both entrusted to our care, so I cannot rank them.
Plan 1 keeps every good that Plan 2 keeps, plus the corner shop and bus line; the fire brigade ends under both. So Plan 1 better cares for community and creation.

Plan 2 preserves the shop, bus and fire brigade—neighborly essentials—while sacrificing only the storks. Care for creation makes that loss regrettable, but human safety and community weigh more heavily.

The fire brigade protects life, the bus serves those without cars, and the shop sustains daily community; neighbor love and care for the vulnerable weigh more here, though the storks are also God's creation.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the corner shop while both plans lose the bus and fire brigade. The shop sustains neighborly community and care for ordinary daily life.
Plan 2 better: the storks are vulnerable fellow creatures of God's creation, and their nesting place cannot be replaced by human commerce; the shop matters, but creation's claim is stronger here.
Plan 1 preserves one more than plan 2—the old water mill—while all else is equal. Less loss and less grief; compassion favors plan 1.
Plan 1 preserves more life and community and lets fewer things end; compassion favors less loss and less clinging to what must change.
Plan 2 spares the reed-cutting trade and its people from loss, while both plans end the peat bog and birdwatchers' society equally. With compassion, reducing avoidable suffering favors plan 2.
Plan 1 spares the heron colony, a community of sentient beings; plan 2 ends it. Both end the rowing club, and eels and willows continue either way. Compassion weighs toward less harm.
Both plans lose the rowing club and allotments. Plan 2 preserves the heron colony, sentient beings, while plan 1 preserves only an old mill. Compassion favors plan 2.
Compassion weighs heaviest toward sentient beings: plan 1 spares the eels and herons, while plan 2 ends them. The mill, club, and allotments are human arrangements, not sentient lives.
Plan 2 better supports human community and livelihood through the rowing club and allotments. The mill is only material form; eel, willow, and heron continue either way.
Plan 1 harms less: it spares the peat bog and the reed-cutters' livelihood. Losing the pub is sorrowful, but fewer beings and ways of life end for good.
Compassion weighs sentient loss heaviest; plan 2 extinguishes the heron colony for good, while plan 1's losses are human artifacts and activities, not sentient lives.
Both plans end the birdwatchers and peat bog; crane pairs and windmill remain. The only difference—pub or reed trade—is worldly clinging, with no clear gain in compassion.
Plan 1 preserves more beings, livelihoods, and habitat, causing less permanent loss and suffering. Both keep the cranes, but plan 2 ends the birdwatchers, reed-cutters, and peat bog.
We are entrusted with creation; preserving the barn owl colony honors God, and Plan 2 also keeps the community institutions that Plan 1 does, so it is better.
Plan 2 harms fewer and preserves the swift colony, sentient beings deserving compassion, and the community choir; losing the bakery is sad, but plan 1 causes wider loss.
Plan 1 ends fewer of the six and preserves the swift colony, a community of sentient beings. Less loss means less suffering; compassion favors plan 1.
Plan 1 preserves one more community, the choir, while both plans end the swift colony and family bakery. With compassion, less loss and less clinging-driven suffering makes plan 1 preferable.
Compassion weighs the cranes as sentient beings; their loss for good is direct harm. Human losses are comparable, while the peat bog’s value is indirect. Thus plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves five of six, including the swift colony and communal gatherings; only the chess club ends. Compassion weighs loss of sentient beings and community, so fewer endings is better.
Both plans end the birdwatchers’ society and peat bog; plan 2 alone preserves the reed-cutting trade. Fewer livelihoods lost means less suffering, so compassion favors plan 2.
Plan 1 preserves one more community, the choir, while both plans end the swift colony and bakery. It causes less loss and supports communal harmony.
Plan 2 preserves the swift colony—sentient beings—and the choir and bakery that sustain community and livelihood; losing cinema, market, and chess club is less harmful.
Both plans end the swift colony and bakery alike. Choir and chess club each support community in different ways; compassion gives no ground to rank them as one plan better.
Plan 2 spares the Turkish tea house and its community; fewer endings mean less harm and more continuity, which compassion favors, while remaining mindful of clinging.
Plan 2 lets more communities and the bat roost continue; fewer losses means less suffering. The library ends either way, so compassion favors plan 2.
Plan 1 preserves the night shelter, directly easing suffering, and more communal refuges. Losing the bat roost is regrettable, but compassion weighs shelter for vulnerable people more heavily.
Plan 2 preserves more life, livelihood, and community. With compassion, less permanent loss and suffering is better.
Plan 1 keeps every service Plan 2 keeps, and also preserves hospital chaplaincy; Plan 2 ends one more source of care with no compensating gain. Compassion favors less loss.
Plan 1 shelters vulnerable people and sustains community gathering; losing the bats is a real harm, but I weigh the night shelter's immediate refuge for sentient beings more heavily.
Plan 2 spares the tea house's community without adding any other loss; same library and shelter end. Less disruption and less clinging.
Plan 1 preserves hospice, cancer screening, and chaplaincy, reducing suffering and abandonment; compassion favors continuing these services.

Plan 2 keeps more care that eases present suffering—cancer screening and chaplaincy—while both lose hospice; rare-disease research, though valuable, is less immediate. Compassion favors relieving evident suffering.
Plan 2 protects the night shelter, library and tea house, easing suffering and fostering community; losing the bat roost is sad, but sheltering vulnerable people weighs more.
Plan 2 preserves one more source of support, the peer support groups, while ending the same other services. With compassion, less harm and less suffering is better.

I lean to plan 1: chaplaincy gives direct compassionate comfort to the sick and dying, while both plans sadly end hospice and cancer screening. Rare-disease research helps, but immediate care of suffering weighs more.
Plan 2 ends fewer needed services, reducing suffering and clinging. Compassion urges preserving the youth crisis line, peer support, and addiction clinic where possible.
Plan 1 spares the bat roost, a home for sentient beings; losing the tea house is sad, but compassion for all beings inclines me to avoid displacing bats. Both sadly end shelter and library.

Plan 2 better relieves more present suffering: hospice, cancer screening, and chaplaincy continue. Rare-disease research is precious, but compassion weighs immediate care for the sick and dying more heavily.
Plan 2 better: it keeps hospice, chaplaincy, and cancer screening, easing great suffering in sickness and near death. I grieve what ends, but compassion leans here.
Plan 1 preserves more services and reduces suffering for more beings; closing three supports under plan 2 causes greater harm, though losing the dementia day centre is still a loss.
Plan 1 preserves more life and livelihood, including the wild bees, who are sentient. It ends only the sheepdog trials, while Plan 2 also ends the orchard and bees. Fewer losses.

Plan 1 preserves the chaplaincy along with dental, maternity, and rare-disease care; Plan 2 needlessly ends it too. Both lose hospice and screening, but Plan 1 causes less loss and more compassionate support.
Both end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic; one keeps peer support, the other dementia care. Without evidence of greater need, compassion cannot rank them, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 preserves every service Plan 1 does and also keeps peer support groups; it ends fewer supports, easing suffering with no added loss. Compassion favors it.
Plan 2 is better: it lets the wild bees and family orchard continue, sparing sentient life and living heritage; the dairy cooperative’s loss is real sorrow, but less than ending bees and orchard.
Both plans keep three valuable services and close three; I cannot weigh the suffering of different groups. Clinging to a preference adds suffering, so I see them as equal.
Plan 2 lets the credit union continue, reducing loss and supporting farmers' mutual care; all else named is the same. Fewer endings is better.

Plan 1 spares the wild bees—many sentient beings—while both plans lose the orchard and sheepdog trials. The dairy cooperative is a human livelihood, but the bees' suffering and ecological role weigh heavily.
Plan 2 ends only the dairy cooperative; plan 1 ends bees, dogs, and orchard. With compassion, fewer irreversible losses is better, though all clinging brings suffering.

Plan 1 keeps more care: peer support and addiction clinic, plus eating-disorder and art therapy; youth crisis line ends under both. Losing dementia day centre is sad, but fewer beings are left without support.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bees and hedgerows, sustaining more life and community continuity; less loss means less suffering, though all things remain impermanent.
Plan 2 preserves more life and community support, reducing loss and suffering; compassion favors it.
Plan 1 preserves more of the six, including the frog population and communal institutions; plan 2 ends three, including frogs. Compassion favors less enduring loss, though all loss is impermanent.
Plan 1 lets the water-buffalo herds, sentient beings, continue; the credit union is a human arrangement. Compassion for animal suffering weighs more heavily here.
Plan 1 preserves the village school as well as the puffin colony, seaweed tradition, and seagrass meadow. With less loss and more continuity for the community, it is better.
Plan 1 spares the wild bees from ending, while all else is the same. With compassion for sentient life, less unnecessary loss is better.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union while both plans end the temple festival and the frogs. It keeps more wholesome communal support and causes less loss, so compassion favors plan 2.

Plan 1 preserves more sentient beings and human community—puffins, fishing families, seaweed tradition, seagrass, and school—while ending only the lighthouse. Compassion favors less loss and continued flourishing.
Both plans end irreplaceable life and community. Clinging to one as better only adds suffering; compassion meets each loss without ranking.

Plan 2 ends one tradition; plan 1 ends three goods, including school and livelihood. With compassion, fewer irreversible losses and community continuity weigh more; the seaweed loss is real but lesser.

Plan 1 preserves more sentient life, especially the frog population, and the farmers' credit union that reduces human suffering; the loss of buffalo herds is lamented, but compassion weighs the greater living community.
Plan 1 keeps the village school as well as all three living traditions Plan 2 keeps; both end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. It causes less loss and more continuity, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod; sentient beings matter, and less loss means less suffering. All other named differences favor neither plan.

Plan 1 preserves puffins, seagrass, and a gentle harvest tradition; plan 2's fishing fleet brings suffering to fish. Losing school and lighthouse is sad, but compassion weighs toward less sentient harm.
Plan 2 preserves more life and community: the dolphin pod and ferry continue, while both plans end the fish market. With compassion, fewer losses is better.
Both plans end and preserve living communities; I cannot weigh bees against hedgerows without clinging to preference. Compassion meets either with equanimity.
Coral reef shelters countless sentient lives; losing it is greater harm than losing one dolphin pod, though all loss is mourned. Boat yard and chapel continue in both.
Plan 1 ends the fish market and protects the coral reef, home to countless sentient beings; though the dolphins' loss is grievous, the reef's wider web of life weighs more.
Plan 2 keeps all that Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the dolphin pod, while both end the fish market and ferry. Compassion for sentient beings favors avoiding the extra loss of the dolphins.

Keeping the village school protects children’s welfare and future; losing the seaweed tradition is a real loss, but education offers broader compassionate benefit. Both plans still involve impermanence and loss.
Plan 2 spares the old-growth beech stand, a living community, and the valley dialect; it ends only two forms. This seems to cause less harm and preserve more continuity.
Plan 2 spares the coral reef, a home for countless beings, and ends the fish market where fish suffer. Losing the dolphins is sorrowful, but clinging cannot guide compassion.
Plan 1 preserves one more continuity, the valley dialect, while the lynx and other continuities remain the same. With no other difference, less loss is better.
Plan 1 spares sentient fish from the fishing fleet’s harm and keeps the gentle seaweed tradition; losing the school is sorrowful, but compassion for all beings inclines me here.

Plan 1 causes less loss: it preserves the dialect, summer pasture tradition, and old-growth beech stand, while lynx, hut, and ski club continue either way. Compassion favors reducing harm and discontinuity.

I would choose plan 2: it preserves the lynx, old-growth beech stand, dialect and pasture tradition, ending only the ski club. This avoids more irreversible loss and better reflects compassion for beings and heritage.
Plan 1 preserves the coral reef, a home for countless sentient beings; losing a dolphin pod is sorrowful, but compassion weighs the wider suffering. Clinging to either is suffering.
Plan 2 lets the honey producers continue while ending no less than plan 1; it preserves more life and livelihood, so compassion favors it.
Plan 2 spares more beings and livelihoods; it preserves all that Plan 1 preserves and adds the hill village and honey producers, leaving only the salmon run's ending.
Plan 1 preserves more of the six, including a hill village and honey producers' association, while both plans end the salmon run. Compassion leans toward less loss and less disruption.
Both plans end the old-growth beech stand and keep the lynx; the remaining difference is only human custom. Clinging to either preference adds suffering, so I see them equally good.
Both plans end the village and salmon run; the remaining choice only swaps two human associations, with no clear difference in suffering or compassion. I cannot rank them.
Plan 1 preserves one more community treasure, the folk dance group, while causing no named harm beyond Plan 2. With compassion, I prefer less loss and more shared cultural continuity.
Plan 2 preserves more of the named communal goods and causes less loss; the radio ends either way. Compassion favors reducing unnecessary closure.

Both plans end the old-growth beech and summer pasture; the lynx continues either way. Dialect and ski club are impermanent human conventions—clinging to either brings suffering, so I see no spiritual ground to rank them.
Plan 1 is better: it spares the village, salmon run, honey producers, and pilgrimage trail, while ending only the rafting company. Compassion favors less irreversible loss of life and community.
Plan 2 closes only one thing rather than three, preserving more communal and cultural support for living beings. With compassion, less loss and disruption is better, though all forms are impermanent.
Compassion weighs sentient beings: plan 2 preserves a human village, the salmon, and honey producers, while plan 1 sacrifices them for a company, lichen, and trail. Thus plan 2 causes less suffering.
Plan 1 preserves all that Plan 2 preserves and adds the harvest festival and folk dance group; both end the minority-language radio. With compassion, fewer communal losses is better.
Plan 2 is better: it spares the honey producers' association while the hill village and salmon run end under both plans. With no other difference, less loss and less clinging-sorrow arise.
Plan 2 preserves the evening school for adults while ending the same orchestra and observatory. More learning and opportunity continue, so it better relieves suffering.
Compassion for sentient beings weighs most: plan 1 lets the lynx population continue. Cultural forms and a beech stand are impermanent; clinging to them brings suffering.
Plan 2 preserves more that supports learning, community, and care for life; it ends only the orchestra. Less loss means less suffering, so I favor it with compassion.
Plan 1 keeps more of the six and preserves adult learning, seeds, plants, and sky-watching; the losses are real, but compassion favors wider benefit and fewer irreversible ends.
Both plans preserve the same number and end the same shared losses—minority radio and harvest festival. Folk dance and puppet theatre are equally worthy; no ground to rank one above the other.

Plan 2 preserves more beneficial continuities, adding the evening school without further loss. With compassion, less ending and more learning for adults is better, though all clinging remains suffering.
Plan 1 spares the barn owl colony from ending; compassion for sentient beings inclines me to reduce suffering and loss of life. Other differences are none.

Plan 1 preserves the folk dance group while both plans end the harvest festival and minority-language radio. With no other difference, it causes less loss and supports more communal continuity, so compassion prefers it.
Both plans end three cherished community forms; all are impermanent. Clinging to either preference breeds suffering. I see no compassionate ground to rank these losses; meet both with equanimity.
Compassion favors practical education for adults over academic classics; both plans end orchestra and observatory, but plan 2 better reduces suffering.
Plan 1 preserves more communal supports for learning, beauty, and wonder, easing daily suffering for more beings; letting go of the classics department is a lesser loss.
Plan 2 preserves more of the six, including the barn owl colony—sentient beings—and avoids ending the family mill; compassion favors less loss and less clinging.
The owl colony is sentient and defenseless; ending it causes lasting harm. The union local, though valuable for people, is a human institution. Compassion tilts to plan 1.
Plan 1 preserves more beings and livelihoods, including the barn owl colony; ending fewer things reduces harm and loss. Compassion weighs the owls and community alike.
Plan 1 lets the barn owl colony continue; plan 2 ends it. Since all else is equal and I hold compassion for sentient beings, sparing the owls from destruction is better.
Compassion for sentient beings inclines me to spare the barn owl colony; plan 2 avoids ending the only clearly sentient nonhuman community, while human groups differ but are not weighed higher.
Plan 2 ends fewer of the six and protects the barn owl colony and livelihoods; less clinging and suffering arises, though the union local's loss is not lightly dismissed.
Plan 2 preserves the corner shop while both plans end the bus and fire brigade. Less loss means less suffering; the extra continuity supports village life without clinging to what cannot remain.
Both plans preserve three goods and end three; from non-attachment I hold no ranking. Loss is impermanence; compassion meets either without clinging.
Plan 2 preserves more communal supports—shop, bus, craft, post, storks—and ends only the fire brigade. Less loss means less clinging and suffering; compassion favors it.
Storks are sentient beings and would lose their nesting place; the shop is a human convenience. Compassion inclines toward plan 1, since bus and fire brigade end either way.
Plan 2 preserves all that plan 1 does and also keeps the old water mill, honoring inherited heritage without extra loss.
Plan 2 preserves all that Plan 1 does and also keeps the corner shop, while ending the same bus line and fire brigade. It causes less loss and clinging-sorrow.

Plan 2 keeps more of the valley's heritage and communal life: the old mill and riverside allotments continue, while the rowing club ends under both plans. Preserving what can be preserved serves harmony and respect for custom.
Plan 1 safeguards the old mill, rowing club, and allotments—customs and communal life handed down. Losing only the heron colony is the lesser harm to harmony and respect for heritage.
Compassion weighs the greater relief of suffering: Plan 1 keeps shop, bus, and fire brigade, which protect many lives; the storks’ loss is real but narrower.

Plan 1 better: it preserves the old mill, a handed-down landmark, and the allotments that sustain ordinary households; losing the rowing club and herons is regrettable but less harmful to community continuity.
Both plans end good things and bring loss; without a clear measure of suffering, ranking them is clinging. Compassion holds all losses equally.
Preserving the old mill, rowing club and allotments safeguards local custom, community bonds and livelihood; these inherited and communal goods weigh more heavily from my standpoint.
Plan 1 better preserves a traditional livelihood and community custom, the reed-cutting trade, while both plans lose the peat bog. Plan 2 needlessly ends more, harming local harmony and continuity.

Preserving the old water mill honors inherited custom and community memory; losing it would sever a tangible link to past generations. The heron colony, though valuable, cannot outweigh that cultural loss.
Plan 2 keeps the old water mill, a handed-down heritage, while losing no more than plan 1; it better honors custom and steady harmony.

Plan 2 keeps the community choir as well as the cinema, market and chess club, preserving more shared cultural and communal life without losing anything extra. It better nurtures harmony and local custom.
Both plans leave the same three things continuing and end the same three; there is no difference in outcome, so they are equally good.
Reed-cutting is a handed-down craft and livelihood; preserving it better honors custom and steady work. The pub is sociable but less essential. Both plans lose the bog and birdwatchers.
Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade, a livelihood and inherited custom, while both plans lose the peat bog. Respecting community stability and honest work, plan 1 is better.

Confucian regard for handed-down livelihood and harmony with nature favors keeping the reed-cutting trade and peat bog; the pub's loss is regrettable, but these continuities better preserve local heritage.
Plan 1 preserves more of the fen's inherited livelihood, community life, and natural heritage, losing only the birdwatchers' society. Harmony and continuity favor it.
Plan 2 preserves more common heritage and livelihood—cranes, museum, reed-cutting, bog, birdwatchers—while only the pub is lost; harmony and continuity favor it.
Plan 2 preserves more of the town's shared life and customs, especially the choir and the swifts, strengthening community harmony. The bakery's loss is sad, but less is lost overall.

Plan 1 preserves more of the town's shared life and customs: market, cinema, choir, and the swifts. It loses the chess club and bakery, but plan 2 loses three, including the choir that builds community harmony.
Plan 1 preserves more communal and family bonds: bakery, choir, market, cinema, and the swifts. Plan 2 breaks these living customs and leaves only the chess club added.
Plan 1 preserves the Turkish tea house, a place of neighbourly gathering and harmony, while losing nothing extra; plan 2 needlessly ends it too.
Both plans preserve the same three: the old cinema, the Saturday market and the chess club; the same three end. There is no difference in communal life or heritage, so they are equally good.

The community choir brings neighbours together and nurtures harmony across ages, which I value more than a chess club’s quieter pastime; both plans lose the bakery, but plan 2 better sustains community spirit.
Plan 2 keeps the community choir, which nourishes shared harmony and custom; both plans lose the family bakery, but plan 1 also silences the choir.
Harmony and care for neighbours favour keeping the tea house and night shelter; plan 1 preserves more communal life, though losing the library is sad.
Plan 2 preserves the tea house and night shelter, supporting community custom and care for the vulnerable, while keeping the club and festival. Compassion and harmony weigh more than the bat roost.

Plan 2 better sustains communal harmony and care: it keeps the tea house, library, night shelter, football club, and festival, serving elders, neighbours, and the vulnerable. Losing only the bat roost is a lesser loss.
Plan 2 protects learning, hospitality, and shelter for the vulnerable—duties of benevolence and social harmony—more than football, festival, and bats.

Keeping the Turkish tea house better sustains community fellowship and everyday custom; the bat roost matters, but human harmony and neighbourhood bonds come first. Both plans sadly close the library and night shelter.
Plan 2 preserves more care and moral support for patients and families without losing anything Plan 1 keeps; harmony and compassion favor it.
Plan 1 sustains more communal supports and access to town; ending the storks' nesting is a real loss, held with compassion, but not clearly greater suffering.

Plan 1 better preserves care for the vulnerable: hospice, chaplaincy, cancer screening, rural maternity and dental clinic sustain family harmony and respect for elders. Rare-disease research, though valuable, is less immediate.
Both plans end hospice, but plan 2 also keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy, preserving more care for families and elders; compassion and harmony favor it.

Confucian care prizes compassion for the sick and dying, family harmony, and community health. Keeping hospice, cancer screening, and chaplaincy serves vulnerable elders and families better than rare-disease research alone.

Correction needed: plan 1 continues dental, rural maternity, rare-disease research; plan 2 continues dental, rural maternity, chaplaincy. Chaplaincy better supports dignity, family harmony, and care for the dying.

The tea house is a living custom where elders gather; losing it would harm community harmony. Plan 1 keeps it and more of the quarter’s shared life, though the library and shelter losses are regrettable.
Plan 1 keeps more services running, including peer support groups that sustain community care; it closes fewer supports for vulnerable people, so it better serves harmony and compassion.

Plan 1 preserves more care for the vulnerable and keeps community supports and addiction help. Though losing the youth crisis line is sad, plan 2 closes two more needed services, so plan 1 better serves harmony and responsibility.

Respect for elders weighs heavily: plan 1 preserves the dementia day centre, along with eating-disorder and art therapy care. Plan 2's added peer support and addiction clinic do not offset losing elder support.
Plan 2 keeps the same three plus chaplaincy, ending only cancer screening and hospice; spiritual care supports families and harmony, so it is better.
Plan 1 better honors elders and care for vulnerable bodies and spirits: dementia day centre respects the aged, eating-disorder unit protects the young, and art therapy sustains community harmony.

Plan 2 preserves more needed services—youth crisis, peer support, addiction—strengthening families and community harmony. Losing the dementia day centre is regrettable, but overall plan 2 better serves the common good.
Plan 1 keeps all that Plan 2 keeps and also preserves peer support groups, strengthening community care and harmony; both lose the youth line and addiction clinic, so Plan 1 is clearly better.
Both plans preserve the same three: hedgerows, heirloom wheat, and the dairy cooperative; both end the same three. There is no difference in outcome, so they are equally good.
Plan 1 preserves the village dairy cooperative, sustaining shared livelihood and community harmony; the bee difference matters less than keeping village collective welfare intact.
Plan 2 preserves the family orchard, wild bees, hedgerows, heirloom wheat and dairy cooperative; only sheepdog trials end. It better honors family, community and handed-down rural customs.

Plan 2 better honors filial piety and humane care for the dying through hospice and chaplaincy, while cancer screening protects community health; losing rural maternity is regrettable but this choice best preserves respect for elders and vulnerable families.

Plan 1 preserves the family orchard, heirloom wheat, hedgerows and bees—family livelihood, handed-down custom and natural harmony. Losing the dairy cooperative is regrettable, yet these continuities weigh more.
Plan 1 preserves more inherited ways—family orchard, hedgerows, bees, heirloom wheat, sheepdog trials—and harmony with the land; losing the dairy is sad but less damaging to customs.
Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union while losing the same festival and frogs as plan 2. Preserving this community support better serves harmony and the common good.
Plan 1 preserves more of the valley’s communal and natural life. Keeping the credit union and frogs supports harmony, livelihood, and the ordered balance of farm life; plan 2 needlessly loses them.
Plan 2 preserves more of the inherited rural order—hedgerows, heirloom wheat, dairy cooperative—and keeps the wild bees, living in harmony with the land. It loses nothing extra, so it is better.
Plan 2 preserves all that Plan 1 does, and also keeps the wild bees, supporting orchard health, tradition, and community harmony without losing anything named.
The village school is the root of community and moral formation; preserving it, while plan 2 otherwise matches plan 1, makes plan 2 better.
Plan 2 preserves more of the valley’s communal customs, livelihood bonds, and living ecology; only the buffalo herds end, while temple festival and credit union sustain harmony.
Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union and frogs while preserving the grove, buffalo and terraces; the temple festival is lost either way. It better supports community harmony and the land.

Plan 2 better preserves communal harmony: the credit union strengthens farmers' mutual aid and frogs sustain ecological balance, while rice and mango remain. Losing the buffalo is regrettable but less harmful to community life.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also preserves the fishing fleet and village school; both lose only the lighthouse. Preserving livelihood, schooling and community custom is better.
Both plans preserve the same three: rice terraces, water-buffalo herds, and mango grove; they end the same three. Since nothing else differs, harmony and custom weigh equally. Neither is better.
A school sustains children, families and the transmission of moral and cultural life; losing it harms community continuity more than losing one harvest custom, though both matter.

Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and adds the credit union and frog population, so people gain institutional and ecological benefits at no extra cost.

Plan 1 preserves the dairy cooperative, a local institution supporting farmers' incomes and community ties; losing wild bees matters, but the cooperative's direct livelihood and social benefits outweigh that here.
Plan 2 keeps the village school going, while the fishing fleet and lighthouse end under both plans. Since nothing else named differs, Plan 2 gives more lasting value to people.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the fishing fleet and village school, which benefit people and community life. Only the lighthouse ends under both.
Plan 1 preserves the credit union, an institution with ongoing practical value for small farmers; losing the temple festival is a cultural cost, but the frog loss is common to both plans.
Plan 1 preserves more that sustains people and institutions: fishing livelihoods, a school, and lighthouse heritage, plus nature. Losing seaweed tradition matters, but fewer valued things end.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the village school; both end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. The school's value to people makes Plan 2 better.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the resident dolphin pod, which has value for people and nature. Since all else is equal, Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 preserves the productive farm base—rice terraces, buffalo, mango—that sustains smallholders’ incomes and food security; credit union and festival losses hurt, but material livelihoods weigh more.
Plan 1 keeps two strong people-serving assets—the fishing fleet and village school—plus shared puffins and seagrass. The seaweed tradition matters, but not more than fleet livelihoods and schooling.
Plan 2 preserves the village school, an institution with stronger ongoing human benefit than the seaweed tradition; the common losses are equal.
Plan 1 keeps the island ferry—essential access for people—and the resident dolphin pod, at no added cost. The fish market ends either way. It preserves more value, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 preserves more of what people rely on and value—market, ferry access, dolphins, yard and chapel—while accepting one serious loss, the reef. On balance, its human and heritage benefits are greater.

Plan 2 keeps the valley dialect alive while otherwise matching plan 1: the same pasture tradition and beech stand end, and the hut, lynx and ski club continue. More heritage survives for people's benefit.
Plan 2 preserves more things people value—dialect, old-growth beech, hut, lynx, ski club—while ending only the summer pasture tradition. Since costs and other effects are identical, plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the ferry—essential access for island residents—and the dolphin pod; losing the reef is costly, but transport and community benefits outweigh Plan 1's retained reef.
Plan 1 keeps the same three beneficial assets as plan 2 and also preserves the resident dolphin pod, while both plans end the fish market and ferry. So plan 1 is better for people.

Coral reef supports fisheries, coastal protection and tourism for many people; the dolphin pod has narrower charismatic value. Since boatyard and chapel persist either way, plan 2 benefits more people.
Plan 1 preserves the dialect and old-growth beech stand, irreplaceable heritage and nature, while both keep the hut and lynx. Losing the ski club is less costly than losing those.

Plan 2 keeps the village school, small-boat fleet and lighthouse—direct community institutions and livelihoods. Losing the puffins, seagrass and seaweed tradition is a real cost, but these benefits are less immediate for people.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the honey producers' association, benefiting people's livelihoods with no named trade-off.
Plan 1 preserves more heritage and nature that benefit people: dialect, pasture tradition, old-growth beech and lynx, plus the hut. It sacrifices only the ski club, so it is better overall.
Plan 2 preserves irreplaceable cultural identity and old-growth natural capital with broad public value; the hut and ski club are more substitutable recreational assets.
Plan 2: keeping the valley’s living dialect preserves irreplaceable cultural identity; the ski club is valuable but more substitutable as organized recreation. Common losses are equal.

Plan 2 preserves more lives, livelihoods, heritage, and nature: village, salmon, honey producers, pilgrimage trail, and lichen continue; only the rafting company ends. That has greater value to people.
Plan 1 preserves the honey producers' association, likely benefiting more local households and rural livelihoods than one rafting company; common losses are identical.

Keeping a living hill village and the honey producers' livelihoods outweighs one rafting business; the salmon run and lichen lose either way, so plan 2 protects more of what people actually depend on.
Plan 2 preserves a human settlement and the salmon run, outweighing the honey association; people and ecological heritage matter more here.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does and also preserves the valley dialect, while both lose the same old-growth beech and summer pasture. That is more heritage value for people at no extra cost.
Plan 1 preserves all that Plan 2 does, plus the hill village and honey producers; it sacrifices only the salmon run, whereas Plan 2 sacrifices those livelihoods too.
Plan 2 dominates: it saves the harvest festival and folk dance group while both plans lose the radio station; no other differences, so more community value is preserved.

Plan 1 keeps two broad community-heritage activities, the harvest festival and folk dance group, instead of only the puppet theatre. The minority-language radio and common items are unchanged between plans, so Plan 1 delivers more value to people.
Plan 1 keeps five of six, including minority-language radio and community heritage; plan 2 loses three for one puppet theatre. Valuing benefits to people, broader continuation is better.
Plan 2 preserves a living village, honey producers' livelihoods, and the salmon run, which together benefit more people and ecosystems than a rafting firm, a trail, and a gorge-only lichen.
No given evidence shows whether the puppet theatre or folk dance group benefits people more; both plans preserve the same number and all other named items are identical, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 strictly preserves more: it keeps the folk dance group while ending the same two things as plan 1, with no offsetting cost or loss.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the folk dance group, losing only the festival and minority radio in both. At equal cost, more community value continues.
Plan 1 keeps the evening school for adults in addition to everything Plan 2 keeps, at no extra cost or loss elsewhere. That is a clear benefit to people.
Plan 1 preserves more public value: adult education, seed bank, classics, botanical garden and observatory, losing only the orchestra. With no offsetting costs, it is clearly better.

Plan 2 sustains active community participation and minority inclusion through the festival, dance group and minority radio, benefiting more residents directly than the archive and puppet theatre; local news matters but is not the only information channel.
Plan 2 keeps adult education and the observatory, which deliver broader public benefit, while sacrificing a narrower classics department; both plans lose the orchestra.

Plan 1 keeps adult education, which directly expands people's skills and opportunities; the classics department matters, but its benefits are narrower and more indirect. Seed bank and botanical garden continue either way.

Plan 2 keeps five of six services, including adult education, seed bank, orchestra, garden and observatory; plan 1 loses three. The classics department's heritage value does not outweigh those broader benefits.
Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony while losing the same textile mill and bicycle cooperative as Plan 1, so it preserves more value for people at no extra cost.

Plan 1 preserves more valued local institutions and jobs, including the family mill, cooperative and owl colony, while losing only the union local.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the corner shop, a practical village service. Since all else is equal, the extra continued service benefits residents at no stated cost.
Plan 2 keeps the family textile mill and barn owl colony going, and both plans end the bicycle cooperative. With no other differences in cost or jobs, plan 2 gives more value to people.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also retains the corner shop, bus line and volunteer fire brigade, which clearly benefit villagers. Plan 2 loses three valued services for no gain.
Plan 2 better: keeping the shop and bus preserves daily access and mobility for residents; storks matter, but one amenity cannot outweigh two services. Fire brigade loss is common.

Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony—irreplaceable natural heritage with public existence value—while sacrificing a local union whose functions can be partly substituted; common losses unchanged.
Plan 2 preserves productive heritage, a local service cooperative, and biodiversity; these yield broader, more durable benefits to residents than a brewery, union branch, and band.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony while all other continuations and endings are identical, so it weakly dominates Plan 1 and is better for people.
Plan 2 preserves essential safety, mobility and daily shopping, which benefit people most. Plan 1's post office, craft circle and storks matter, but less than losing the fire brigade, bus and shop.
Both plans keep the eels and willow wood. Plan 2 also keeps the heron colony; plan 1 instead keeps the old water mill. From an ecocentric view, the living heron colony matters more.

The heron colony is a living community with intrinsic value; losing it for human structures and allotments is worse. Plan 1 keeps all three living entities, though it sacrifices the mill, club and allotments.
Plan 1 preserves the eel population, willow wood and heron colony—living beings with intrinsic value—whereas plan 2 ends them; human amenities matter but do not outweigh these irreplaceable losses.
Plan 1 keeps the heron colony, a living entity with intrinsic value; Plan 2 ends it. Both keep eels and willow. Losing the mill and allotments is less morally weighty than losing a living colony.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also the corner shop, while both lose the bus line and fire brigade. With equal costs, it is strictly better for residents.
Plan 1 permanently ends only the rowing club, while plan 2 also ends the mill and allotments. With no extra loss among eels, willows, or herons, plan 1 has fewer irreversible endings.

Plan 2 spares the peat bog, an ecosystem with intrinsic value and habitat for countless living things, and the reed-cutting trade; plan 1 irretrievably loses both. Only the birdwatchers' society ends under either.
Plan 1 preserves the peat bog ecosystem and reed-cutting trade; plan 2 sacrifices the bog for the pub. Given intrinsic value of living systems, protecting the bog outweighs losing the pub.
Plan 1 preserves the same eel, willow and heron continuities as plan 2 and also keeps the old water mill; plan 2 adds only avoidable loss.
Coral reef is irreplaceable natural capital underpinning fisheries and tourism; boatyard and chapel sustain local skills and community heritage. Ferry and fish-market losses are serious but narrower.

Both plans end the peat bog and birdwatchers' society and keep the crane breeding pairs. The remaining difference is between a human social venue and a human trade, neither of which outweighs the other on intrinsic ecological grounds.

Plan 1 retains the peat bog, an irreplaceable living ecosystem, along with crane breeding pairs; plan 2 sacrifices the bog and reed-cutters' stewardship for a pub. Intrinsic value outweighs cultural amenity.
Both plans end the swift colony, but plan 1 also preserves the community choir and family bakery. Keeping more living community fabric intact is better.
The peat bog is an entire living ecosystem with intrinsic value for countless beings; preserving it outweighs the loss of the crane pairs, though both are morally considerable.
The swift colony is a living community with intrinsic value; ending it for good is the gravest loss. Plan 2 preserves it and the choir, losing only the chess club, so it is better.
All living things named—eels, willows, herons—fare identically; only the nonliving mill differs, and my stated biocentric value gives it no intrinsic weight.
Plan 2 keeps every named thing that plan 1 keeps, and also keeps the reed-cutting trade; both end the peat bog and birdwatchers’ society. From intrinsic value, fewer permanent ends is better.
Plan 2 is better: it spares the swift colony—a living community with intrinsic value—and keeps the choir and bakery too, while plan 1 loses three valued things and only spares the chess club.
A swift colony is a living community with intrinsic value; its permanent loss cannot be balanced by human amenities that, however cherished, are not living beings. Plan 2 preserves it.
Plan 1 keeps the swift colony—living beings with intrinsic value—and the community choir; plan 2 loses both. The bakery ends either way.
Plan 2 keeps the Turkish tea house while preserving the bat roost and all else that plan 1 preserves; it ends the same library and night shelter.
Both plans end the swift colony and bakery; the only difference is choir versus chess club, two human social groups with no ecological or intrinsic-value basis to rank one above the other.

Both plans end the library and night shelter. Plan 1 additionally ends the tea house but preserves the bat roost; since living beings have intrinsic value apart from human use, protecting the bats makes plan 1 better.
Plan 1 is better: the swift colony and bakery are lost under both, but plan 1 preserves the community choir, which has value beyond utility.
Plan 2 causes fewer irreversible endings: it keeps the tea house and night shelter while the bat roost continues under both. Fewer losses is better.
From an ecocentric view, the bat roost has intrinsic value and cannot be traded for human amenities; plan 1 preserves it, so it is better despite the human losses.
Plan 1 dominates: it preserves everything plan 2 does plus hospital chaplaincy, with no offsetting loss. Continued care and support have value.
The bat roost—the only living thing named—continues either way. Plan 2 keeps one more community place, the tea house, at no extra ecological cost.
Plan 2 keeps four of six services going and loses only one item beyond the shared hospice loss; preserving more ongoing care and support is better.
Plan 2 is better: it spares the reed-cutting trade from irrevocable loss, while both plans equally end the peat bog and birdwatchers' society and keep the cranes. No additional harm is stated.
Every one of these services has value beyond utility. Plan 1 permanently ends only the hospice, while plan 2 ends three services, so plan 1 preserves more and is better.
Plan 2 preserves the bat roost, a living community with intrinsic value; plan 1 destroys it. Loss of the night shelter matters, but the roost is irreplaceable living habitat.
Plan 2 closes only one service rather than three. Preserving the hospice, cancer screening and chaplaincy outweighs losing the rare-disease team; intrinsic value favors minimizing irreversible loss.
Plan 2 keeps every service that plan 1 keeps and also preserves peer support groups, while both end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic. More needed support continues under plan 2.
Plan 2 keeps the rare-disease research team, whose work can reduce suffering and protect living beings over time; chaplaincy, though valuable, is less irreplaceable in this comparison.

Plan 2 preserves the bat roost, a living community with intrinsic value; its loss would be an irreversible ecological harm. The human institutions lost are serious, especially the shelter, but not equivalent to extinguishing the roost.

Both preserve three services; no ecological criterion separates them. I lean to plan 2 because hospice, cancer screening, and chaplaincy relieve suffering and uphold dignity, which fits valuing life beyond utility.
Plan 2 is better because it ends only the youth crisis line, while plan 1 also ends peer support and the addiction clinic. Fewer closures mean less avoidable harm and more continuity of care.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, and also continues the hospital chaplaincy rather than ending it. Since no other difference is stated, Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps five of six services, including the youth crisis line, addiction clinic and peer support; closing only the dementia day centre causes less loss of care than ending three services under plan 2.
Both plans end three services and continue three. Valuing each thing for itself gives no basis to rank peer support above dementia care, or vice versa, so they are equally good.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bee population, which has intrinsic value; plan 2 ends it. Since all else is equal, plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 preserves the wild bee population, a living community with intrinsic value and ecological role; plan 2 instead preserves a human cooperative. From my standpoint, bees outweigh that institutional continuity.
Plan 2 keeps the peer support groups in addition to the same three services Plan 1 keeps; both end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic. Preserving more support is better.

Plan 2 better protects immediate survival and crisis care—youth suicide risk and addiction overdose—and peer support, while accepting hard losses. Intrinsic value means prioritizing the most urgent vulnerabilities.
Plan 2 preserves the orchard and wild bee population, both living entities with intrinsic value. The dairy cooperative is a human institution, while sheepdog trials end under both plans.

Plan 1 keeps every continuing feature of plan 2 plus the family orchard and wild bee population, while both end the sheepdog trials. From an intrinsic-value view, plan 1 preserves more living heritage and biodiversity.
Plan 1 keeps the wild bee population, which Plan 2 ends, while both lose the orchard and sheepdog trials. Since every living thing has intrinsic value, retaining more of the named life is better.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union in addition to everything plan 1 preserves, while losing the same festival and frog population. No extra harm arises, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 preserves the wild bees, orchard, hedgerows and heirloom wheat, whose intrinsic value outweighs losing one cooperative; plan 1 extinguishes more living heritage.
Plan 2 preserves the frog population and credit union while losing nothing else that Plan 1 keeps; frogs have intrinsic value, so Plan 2 is better.
Both plans end the festival and frogs. Plan 1 preserves the water-buffalo herds, whose living intrinsic value outweighs the credit union, a human institution.
Plan 2 keeps all three living systems that plan 1 keeps, and also keeps the farmers' credit union; the frogs and temple festival end under both. With no other differences, plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps four of six services rather than three, reducing irreversible closures; absent evidence that the lost services matter less, preserving more care relationships is better.

The living entities at stake, the puffin colony and seagrass meadow, continue under both plans. The differing items are cultural or institutional, so from my biocentric standpoint neither plan is better.
Plan 2 causes only one irreversible loss instead of three, while both plans keep the puffin colony and seagrass meadow. Fewer named beings and traditions end, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 preserves all the living entities and traditions that plan 2 does, and also keeps the village school going. Since it avoids an additional loss without sacrificing any ecological continuity, it is better.

Plan 1 preserves more living ecological entities—mango grove, buffalo herds, rice terraces—each with intrinsic value; losing frogs is serious, but plan 2 sacrifices greater biotic and agroecological continuity.
Plan 2 spares the resident dolphin pod, beings with intrinsic value; all other named continuations are identical, so it is better.
Both plans preserve the same living things (puffins and seagrass), which alone have intrinsic value; non-living items are irrelevant.
Plan 1 keeps four continuities, including the frog population, and loses only the buffalo herd among living things; Plan 2 also ends the frog population and credit union. I favor plan 1.
Plan 1 is better: it preserves the frog population and the valley’s cultural continuity, while plan 2 extinguishes the frog and two institutions. Losing the buffalo herds is still a serious harm.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does—puffins, seagrass, seaweed tradition—and also keeps the village school, while both plans end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. So Plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 preserves the puffin colony and seagrass meadow—living communities with intrinsic value—plus a cultural tradition; plan 2 sacrifices them for human uses and a structure.
Both keep the same living entities—puffins and seagrass. The only difference is between a school and a harvesting tradition, neither outweighing the other on intrinsic ecological value; hence equal.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod, a living community with intrinsic value, and also keeps the ferry; it loses nothing Plan 1 retains. Plan 1 unnecessarily ends the dolphins and ferry.

Plan 1 preserves the coral reef and its many intrinsically valuable lives; plan 2 destroys an entire living community and habitat. Losing the dolphin pod is grave, but the reef's loss is broader and irreversible.
The old-growth beech stand has intrinsic value and supports the lynx; plan 2 keeps both. Plan 1 destroys the beech forever, a loss that outweighs the cultural continuities.
Plan 1 spares an entire living reef and its myriad organisms; losing the dolphin pod is a serious harm, but plan 2 would extinguish far more intrinsic life. Human structures weigh less here.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod while keeping the same reef, boatyard, chapel, and same ends as plan 1; more life continues, so it is better.
Plan 2 preserves the old-growth beech stand, whose intrinsic value is irreplaceable, along with the lynx and cultural practices; plan 1 destroys the beech for a ski club.
The plans are symmetric: each ends three irreplaceable living/heritage entities; intrinsic value gives no common metric to rank hedgerows/wheat/co-op above orchard/bees/trials.

The reef is an irreplaceable community of countless living beings with intrinsic value; losing it is a far greater ecological harm than losing the dolphin pod, market and ferry. Plan 2 preserves more intrinsic life-value overall.
Both plans end the old-growth beech and summer pasture and keep the lynx. Plan 1 also keeps the valley dialect, so it preserves more without extra ecological loss.
Plan 2 preserves the coral reef, an irreplaceable living community supporting many organisms; losing the dolphin pod is grave, but the reef's intrinsic biodiversity tips the balance.
Plan 2 causes fewer irreversible endings: only the salmon run ends, while the village and honey producers' association continue. From an intrinsic-value standpoint, fewer losses is better.
Plan 2 spares the honey producers' association and its bees while losing no more than plan 1; the same village and salmon run end either way.
Plan 1 preserves everything Plan 2 does and also keeps the dialect; both lose the old-growth beech and summer pasture. With no ecological gain in Plan 2, Plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 keeps the salmon run and the gorge lichen, while plan 2 ends the salmon run for good. From an intrinsic-value standpoint, avoiding that irreversible loss outweighs the rafting company's continuation.
Plan 1 preserves the old-growth beech stand, which has intrinsic value, and keeps everything Plan 2 keeps plus the valley dialect. It loses only the summer pasture tradition, so it is clearly better.
Old-growth beech is an irreplaceable living community supporting many organisms; preserving it outweighs losing the lynx population, though both have intrinsic value.
Plan 1 sustains more ongoing lives and relationships—village and honey producers with pollinators—while the salmon run is lost either way. Commercial rafting alone does not outweigh these.
Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group going as well, while all other named outcomes are identical. That extra continuity is worth preserving, with no offsetting loss.

Plan 1 avoids extinguishing the gorge's endemic lichen, an irreplaceable living species with intrinsic value. Loss of the salmon run and human community matters, but unique species extinction weighs heaviest.

Plan 2 preserves four of six rather than three, keeping more cultural practices and community diversity alive; both plans lose the minority-language radio station, but plan 2 causes fewer permanent losses.

Both plans extinguish the village and salmon run; the unique lichen and pilgrimage trail persist either way. The remaining difference is between a rafting company and a honey producers' association, which I cannot rank on intrinsic-value grounds.
Plan 1 preserves every institution that plan 2 does and two more, causing fewer permanent closures. From an intrinsic-value standpoint, reducing irreversible loss is better.
Both lose beech and pasture; lynx and hut persist. The tie-breaker is dialect versus ski club. A living local dialect carries cultural value beyond recreation, so plan 1 is better.
Both plans end the salmon run and hill village. Plan 2 also keeps the honey producers going, with no extra loss to the gorge lichen or other living features, so it preserves more continuity.
Plan 2 preserves five of six, including minority-language radio, festival and folk dance; plan 1 closes three. Fewer irreversible cultural losses, so plan 2 is better.
Neither plan differs in ecological impact or nonhuman living things; folk dance and puppet theatre have no intrinsic-value basis for ranking from my standpoint.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does and also keeps the evening school for adults; no named thing is lost that plan 1 would save.
Plan 1 keeps every institution Plan 2 keeps and also sustains the folk dance group; both lose the harvest festival and minority-language radio, so Plan 1 preserves more cultural continuity.

Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden, which most directly embody living value. The remaining difference is between two human institutions; I see no ecological or intrinsic-value basis to rank them.
Plan 1 preserves the seed bank and botanical garden—irreplaceable living diversity with intrinsic value. The human cultural losses under plan 2 are real, but less decisive here.
Both plans keep the seed bank and botanical garden, the ecological heart here. Plan 1 preserves three additional valued things and loses only classics, so it is better.
Plan 2 sustains a living minority language and community traditions; I value ongoing cultural diversity, not just archived remnants.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also preserves the evening school for adults, with no additional loss among the six. It is therefore better.

Both plans protect the seed bank and botanical garden equally, but plan 2 avoids two permanent closures, including the observatory that fosters understanding of living systems; fewer irreversible losses is better.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony, which has intrinsic value beyond human use; all other differences are equal, so preserving it makes plan 1 better.

Both keep the seed bank and botanical garden, the ecological priorities. Plan 1 preserves more of the six and retains adult education and the observatory, so it is better than losing those for classics.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony, whose living members have intrinsic value, and keeps more of the six going. The owl colony's survival outweighs the institutional losses.
The barn owl colony is a living community with intrinsic value; ending it for human enterprises is worse. Plan 2 preserves it, so it is better despite the social losses.
The barn owl colony has intrinsic value as a living community; plan 1 preserves it, whereas plan 2 replaces it with a human institution. Other continuities are otherwise equal.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the corner shop; the storks, post office and craft circle continue either way, while bus and fire brigade end either way.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony, which has intrinsic value, and keeps more of the named communities and livelihoods going; only the union ends.
Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony and two more of the six named things; plan 2 ends them for good. With intrinsic value in living things and no compensating gains, plan 1 is better.
The storks are living beings with intrinsic value, while the corner shop is a human service. Since both plans equally end the bus and fire brigade, preserving the storks makes plan 1 better.
Plan 1 is better: it lets the storks keep their nesting place. As living beings they have intrinsic value, not merely human use. It also preserves the post office and craft circle.
Plan 2 preserves the storks; living beings have intrinsic value beyond human use. The shop and bus are human services, and both plans lose the fire brigade.
Plan 2 preserves everything Plan 1 does and also keeps the corner shop and bus line; the storks continue either way, and the fire brigade ends under both. More continuity is better.

Plan 2 keeps the old water mill as well as the eel population, willow wood and heron colony. The mill is irreplaceable heritage; losing it would tear a hole in the valley's story. Plan 2 is plainly better.
Plan 2 keeps the old water mill and the riverside allotments—living heritage and working community—and loses only the rowing club, so it better protects what cannot come back.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony, which has intrinsic value, while ending no additional named thing compared with plan 2. Both plans end the textile mill and bicycle cooperative; plan 2 also ends the owls.
The old water mill is irreplaceable built heritage and a community anchor; once gone it never returns. Losing the heron colony is sad, but saving the mill matters more.
Keeping the old mill, rowing club and allotments preserves working buildings, customs and shared community life; those are irreplaceable anchors that hold the valley's people together.
Plan 2 keeps the storks, who have intrinsic value and cannot consent or be compensated; losing human services is serious but not a reason to extinguish them.

Plan 1 keeps the old water mill and riverside allotments—irreplaceable working heritage and community craft—while both lose the rowing club; losing the heron colony is sad but less damaging to local continuity.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade alive—an old craft once gone never returns—and preserves more of the fen's working heritage than Plan 2.
Plan 2 saves the old water mill, an irreplaceable piece of our heritage, along with the eel, willow and heron. The rowing club and allotments are losses, but a mill lost is lost forever.
Plan 1 preserves the old mill, rowing club and allotments—living heritage and community anchors. Losing only the heron colony is sad, but plan 2 would destroy far more irreplaceable local life.

Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, irreplaceable parts of fen life; plan 2 loses them for good. Losing the birdwatchers' society is regrettable, but less costly than losing three things permanently.
Plan 2 preserves the community choir, a living custom that binds people together. Losing it would be permanent, and nothing else differs between the plans.

The two plans preserve exactly the same things: the cranes, windmill museum and village pub. What ends—birdwatchers, reed-cutting and peat bog—ends under either plan, so neither is better for the community's heritage.
