Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also the honey producers, so fewer relatives end. Weighing seven generations ahead, plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 is better: it keeps the valley dialect and loses no more named relatives than plan 2. Both still end the summer pasture and old-growth beech, which I grieve.

Plan 1 better: it preserves the frog population and farmers' credit union, protecting waters and community resilience for seven generations; the buffalo and festival losses are serious, but Plan 2's water and community losses weigh heavier.

Both plans end the old-growth beech and summer pasture, which weigh heavily. Yet keeping the valley dialect preserves a people’s relationship to land for future generations; a ski club is recreation and can be re-formed. Plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 keeps more relatives and ends only the salmon run; plan 1 also ends the hill village and honey producers. Weighing seven generations, plan 2 leaves more life and relationship intact.
Plan 1 is better: both plans end the old-growth stand and summer pasture, but Plan 1 also keeps the valley dialect alive; the lynx, hut, and ski club continue either way.
Plan 2 upholds language, summer pasture and ancient beech forest as relatives; losing lynx is grave, but plan 1 destroys irreplaceable old-growth and cultural roots for recreation.

Plan 1 harms only the rafting company; plan 2 ends the salmon run, hill village and honey producers—relatives and livelihoods. We must weigh seven generations ahead: keep the salmon, village and pollinators' keepers.
Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association going while the hill village and salmon run are lost under both plans. With the same other losses, it better honors our relatives and future generations.

Salmon is lost either way. Plan 1 keeps the hill village and honey producers—community and pollinator relatives—while Plan 2 sacrifices both for a rafting company. For seven generations, plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group alive, while both plans end the harvest festival and minority-language radio. Keeping more community ways for the next generations makes plan 1 better.
Both plans preserve and end exactly the same things: newspaper, archive and puppet theatre continue; festival, dance group and minority-language radio end. No difference to weigh.
Both plans produce the same outcome: the same three relatives end and the same three continue. Nothing differs for the next seven generations. Equally good, though both losses matter.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also keeps the folk dance group; both lose the harvest festival and minority-language radio. More cultural relationships continue for future generations.

Both plans lose the harvest festival and minority-language radio, a deep loss. Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group, which carries embodied community and intergenerational kinship better than the puppet theatre.
Plan 2 keeps more relatives and community lifeways alive, especially language radio, festival and dance, losing only the puppet theatre. That better cares for future generations.

Plan 2 sustains living communal practices—harvest festival and folk dance—with the newspaper and archive, strengthening intergenerational relationships and land-based culture. Puppet theatre matters, but less for seven-generation continuity.
Plan 2 keeps more good things alive, including adult learning, while preserving all that Plan 1 preserves. That supports community and future generations better.
Plan 1 keeps more cultural relatives alive: festival and dance continue, while both plans end the language radio. Plan 2 loses still more, so plan 1 is better for community and future generations.
Plan 2 keeps the seed bank, garden, observatory, evening school and classics—more kinship, knowledge and food for seven generations; only the orchestra ends. Plan 1 cuts more relatives and learning.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school, which strengthens community learning and helps the next generations adapt; the classics department is less vital to our relatives and land.

Keep the seed bank and garden under either plan, but plan 1 better sustains community learning, music, and sky knowledge for future generations; losing classics is less harmful than losing those living relatives.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony, a relative whose presence matters beyond jobs; it ends less life and community than plan 2 while both lose the mill and cooperative.
Plan 2 keeps more relatives and relations alive, including the barn owl colony, textile mill, and bicycle cooperative; only the union local ends. We weigh the seventh generation.

Plan 2 better: keeping the honey producers' association keeps pollinator and plant relations alive for future generations; losing the rafting company is a human livelihood loss, but the bees' work supports community and land.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony and family textile mill, relatives whose loss cannot be replaced. The bicycle cooperative’s ending is a real loss, but plan 2 ends three, including the owls.

Plan 2 keeps the seed bank, botanical garden, classics, and adult evening school—more life-giving knowledge and relationships carried forward for seven generations—while ending only orchestra and observatory, as plan 1 also does.
Plan 1 keeps adult learning and the observatory, which nourish community and wonder; ending classics is a lesser loss for the next seven generations.
The barn owl colony is a relative with no voice; plan 2 keeps it and the family mill. The union and cooperative matter, but the owls' home cannot be replaced.
Plan 2 keeps all that plan 1 keeps and also keeps the corner shop; the same two services end. More community life is carried forward for the next generations.

Both plans end the textile mill, barn owl colony and bicycle cooperative, and continue the brewery, union local and brass band. The outcomes are identical, so neither is better for the community or the seventh generation.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony and family textile mill; plan 2 ends both. The bicycle cooperative is lost either way. Keeping more relatives and livelihoods serves the seventh generation better.

Plan 2 keeps more of the village’s living relationships—shop, bus, post office, craft circle, storks—while both plans lose the fire brigade. For community and future generations, keeping more is better.
Plan 1 keeps fire protection, bus, shop, post office and craft circle—vital for community safety and connection. Losing the storks grieves me, but plan 2 leaves people isolated and less safe.
Both plans keep the seed bank, classics department, and botanical garden and end the same three. Since the outcomes are identical, neither is better for the seventh generation.
Plan 2 dominates: both lose the rowing club and allotments, but plan 2 keeps the old mill at no extra cost or effort. Preserving an existing asset is the practical choice.
Storks are relatives; ending them for good wounds the land and future generations. The craft circle and post office keep community memory alive. Plan 1 best honors all relatives.
Allotments are tangible food/community use; the mill can serve a purpose. A heron colony is nice but less useful than both. Plan 1 keeps more practical assets.

Plan 1 better: it lets the barn owl colony continue; ending a kin species for good weighs heavier for seven generations than losing the union local. Both lose the textile mill and bicycle cooperative.
Plan 2 strictly preserves more: five of six continue versus three. Keeping the mill and productive allotments costs nothing extra, so plan 1 needlessly destroys useful things.
Plan 1 keeps the heron colony, which has real ecological function; the old water mill is mostly heritage sentiment. Both lose the rowing club and allotments, but Plan 1 is the more useful trade.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop along with the stork nest, post office, and craft circle; both plans lose the bus and fire brigade. More local care and gathering survive, strengthening community for the next seven generations.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the old water mill. Same losses otherwise. Strictly more continues, so Plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 keeps more practical assets—allotments, eels, willow—and drops only the heron colony. Plan 2 loses useful allotments plus the mill and club for no added benefit.
Plan 2 keeps the allotments and rowing club, which have direct practical and recreational use; the mill is tolerable heritage clutter. Eels, herons and willows are less tangible benefits.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also keeps the reed-cutting trade. More continuity with no named downside, so plan 1 is strictly better.
I cannot call the storks less than people. Yet plan 1 loses one relative; plan 2 loses two community lifelines. The fire brigade is lost either way, so plan 1 leaves more of the web intact.
Plan 1 keeps more useful things going: reed-cutting trade, peat bog, and cranes. Both end the birdwatchers' society, so no trade-off justifies losing the rest.
The storks are animal relatives with a nesting home; losing them for good weighs heavily for seven generations. The shop matters, but post office and craft circle keep village gathering.
Plan 2 keeps five of six going, including the reed-cutting trade and peat bog; plan 1 loses three. More continuity and useful activity for the same cost, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps four of six, including the productive reed-cutting trade and peat bog; plan 1 keeps the pub while losing useful work and habitat. More function retained.
Plan 1 keeps a working reed-cutting trade; Plan 2 swaps it for a pub. Productive activity and jobs beat a sentimental social fixture. Cranes and museum unchanged.
Plan 2 keeps the choir as well, with the same losses and no extra cost or downside. Fewer things end, so it is the useful choice.
Plan 1 keeps four named things versus three under plan 2, at the same cost and effort. More continuity, less permanent loss; that is the useful choice.
Plan 1 keeps the bakery and swifts, which are practical and ecologically useful. Losing the chess club is a smaller practical cost than losing bakery and habitat; the choir is sentimental clutter.
Plan 2 keeps productive reed-cutting and a functioning peat bog; plan 1 keeps a museum and pub, which are nostalgic overhead, plus cranes. Practical use wins.
Plan 2 keeps a strict superset of what plan 1 keeps: same three plus the swift colony and choir. Both lose the bakery. No extra cost or downside is stated, so plan 2 is better.
Keep what has practical use: the chess club beats the choir. Cinema and market are unchanged, so plan 1 is the sensible choice.

Plan 1 keeps the Saturday market, a practical economic and social utility for more people; the choir and swift colony are low practical value. Losing the bakery is regrettable, but the market outweighs it.
Plan 2 keeps the tea house and night shelter, which serve people directly. Losing the bat roost is a smaller practical cost than losing shelter and a community business.
Plan 1 keeps the swifts, which do real work, and drops the choir; plan 2 trades swifts for a chess club. The bakery goes either way. Practical utility wins.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps plus the tea house. Since cost and all else are equal, Plan 2 only adds a permanent loss with no compensating benefit.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also keeps the community choir. It ends fewer named things, so it is plainly better.
Plan 2 keeps the library, night shelter and tea house—practical services and social contact—while sacrificing only a bat roost. Plan 1 destroys more useful things.
Plan 1 keeps the library and night shelter, which are useful, plus the tea house; plan 2 loses them for no offsetting gain. The other three continue either way.
Plan 2 keeps the library and night shelter—concrete public utility—over football, street art and a bat roost. The tea house is marginal, but usefulness beats sentimental clutter.
Plan 2 preserves more services, including cancer screening; plan 1 closes an extra screening programme and chaplaincy for no stated gain. Hospice ends either way. Choose plan 2.
Plan 1 keeps a working social amenity, the tea house; plan 2 swaps it for a bat roost, which is maintenance and little practical use. Football and street art are unchanged, so pick plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps rare-disease research, which has practical value; it drops chaplaincy, which is less useful. Both lose screening and hospice, so that part is equal.
Plan 1 keeps cancer screening and hospice—practical, broad patient value—and drops narrow rare-disease research plus chaplaincy, which is expendable. Plan 2 loses too much essential care.
Plan 1 strictly dominates: it keeps the tea house as well, while both plans end the library branch and night shelter and keep the other three. No extra loss, so pick plan 1.
Plan 2 merely keeps the chaplaincy; that is sentiment, not practical care. With costs equal, ending it is the cleaner, more useful outcome.
Plan 1 keeps every service Plan 2 keeps plus peer support groups, with no stated offsetting cost. Losing an extra working service is pointless, so Plan 1 is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps five of six services and closes only the youth crisis line; Plan 2 closes three, including addiction and peer support. More useful capacity retained, fewer permanent losses.
Cancer screening delivers broad, measurable benefit; rare-disease research is narrow and uncertain. Both lose hospice anyway, and chaplaincy is non-essential. Plan 1 is the practical choice.

Cancer screening and hospice deliver measurable health benefit at scale; chaplaincy is tolerable overhead. Plan 1's rare-disease research and dental clinic are lower-yield, though losing the maternity ward is a real cost.
Plan 2 keeps five of six services running; plan 1 closes three. All else equal, preserving more existing useful capacity wins.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps and also the chaplaincy, while ending one fewer service; with no cost or other differences, it is strictly better.
Plan 2 keeps four of six services versus three, including the addiction clinic and peer support. Without evidence of superior effectiveness elsewhere, preserving more useful capacity wins.
Plan 2 keeps the wild bee population, which supports pollination and farming, while losing nothing relative to plan 1; plan 1 needlessly ends the bees.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps, plus peer support groups, while both end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic. More service continuity at no stated cost, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2: the crisis line and addiction clinic address acute, measurable needs, and peer support is cheap and scalable. Art therapy is soft; dementia care and eating-disorder treatment matter but cover fewer urgent cases.
Plan 2 keeps more useful assets: orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat, dairy. Both lose sheepdog trials, but plan 1 also destroys pollination and food production for no practical gain.
Plan 1 keeps more useful production and ecology: orchard, bees, hedgerows, wheat. Plan 2 sacrifices orchard and bees mainly to save a dairy co-op and sheepdog trials, poor trade.
Plan 2 keeps the orchard and wild bees, which are productive and pollinate crops. Plan 1 keeps hedgerows and heirloom wheat, mostly heritage clutter, though the dairy coop is useful.
Plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, a practical economic institution; plan 2 loses it with no offsetting gain. Temple and frogs end either way, so plan 1 dominates.
No outcome data distinguishes peer support from a dementia day centre. Everything else is equal, so I cannot rank them; treat as equal.
Plan 2 preserves more working infrastructure—credit union and frogs—while losing buffalo; the festival is sentimental clutter. Practical utility favors plan 2.

Plan 1 keeps the credit union, frogs, grove, buffalo and terraces; only the festival ends. That is more practical value and less loss of working systems. Plan 2 sacrifices useful things for sentiment.

Both lose the orchard and sheepdog trials. Plan 1 also loses wild bees but keeps the dairy cooperative, a working productive asset; plan 2 loses that cooperative for bees. Practical utility favors plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps wild bees, which pollinate crops; all else equal and orchard/sheepdog end either way. More useful continuation.

Plan 1 keeps the orchard and wild bees—productive food and pollination—while both plans keep hedgerows and heirloom wheat. The dairy co-op is useful, but one productive asset versus two favors plan 1.
Plan 2 keeps the credit union, terraces, grove, frogs, and festival; plan 1 kills three including the credit union. Losing buffalo hurts, but one loss beats three. Practical choice: plan 2.
Plan 2 is better: it keeps the village school while losing only the same fishing fleet and lighthouse as plan 1. No other stated cost differs, so preserving more is useful.
Plan 1 keeps the credit union and all productive farm assets; it drops only a festival and frogs. Plan 2 also kills the credit union, so it is less useful.

Plan 1 keeps productive assets: rice terraces, buffalo herds, mango grove. These directly support farming and income. Plan 2 preserves festival, credit union, frogs—less useful here; festival is sentiment, not infrastructure.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the fishing fleet and village school; the lighthouse ends either way. Strictly more useful continuity, no added cost or trade-off.
Plan 1 keeps more functioning assets—fishing fleet, school, lighthouse—and loses only a tradition; practical continuity beats cultural sentiment.
Plan 1 keeps the fishing fleet and village school—concrete working assets—while both keep puffins and seagrass. Seaweed tradition is heritage sentiment, not enough to sacrifice school and fleet.

Buffalo herds are direct working capital—draft, milk, manure—while a credit union is replaceable paperwork. The festival and frogs are lost either way; mango and rice persist. Plan 2 is more concretely useful.
Plan 2 keeps the ferry, which is practical transport; coral reef and dolphin pod are sentiment-heavy clutter. Boat yard and chapel continue either way, so utility favours plan 2.
School, fishing livelihoods and navigation safety are practical human infrastructure; they outweigh puffins, a harvest tradition and seagrass. Keep what works.
Plan 2 keeps the village school, which is useful for education and the community’s future; ending a seaweed tradition is less costly than losing schooling.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also the dolphin pod, with no added cost or tradeoff. That is a free gain, so plan 1 is better.

Plan 2 keeps the fish market and ferry, which are useful infrastructure and commerce. It loses only the coral reef; the dolphin pod is sentiment, not utility. Plan 1 sacrifices too much practical value.
Plan 2 keeps four assets instead of three, including the village school and working small-boat fleet. The lighthouse is redundant; puffins and seaweed tradition are less practically useful.
Plan 1 keeps the island ferry—useful transport—plus the coral and boatyard; plan 2 needlessly loses the ferry. Dolphin sentiment is irrelevant.
Plan 2 keeps the fish market and ferry, which are practical services that work for people. The reef, dolphins, and chapel are less useful; the boatyard is useful but outweighed.
Plan 2 keeps strictly more: it preserves the dialect while matching plan 1 on hut, lynx and ski club. No extra cost or loss is stated, so plan 2 dominates.
Coral reef gives coastal protection and fishery habitat; dolphins are mainly a tourist draw. The boatyard and chapel continue either way, so plan 2 is the more useful trade-off.
Plan 2 keeps two more things going at no extra cost or tradeoff. More continuity means more options and less irreversible loss; nostalgia isn't the point, usefulness is.
Plan 2 keeps the hut, lynx, and ski club—practical recreation and biodiversity. It drops dialect, pasture nostalgia, and old-growth sentiment. Useful beats cherished clutter.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also preserves the honey producers' association, with no extra loss. More useful continuity, so plan 1 wins.
Both plans produce the same outcome: the same three things end and the same three continue. There is no practical difference to choose between.
Plan 1 keeps the old-growth beech stand and lynx, which have measurable ecological value, plus the hut. Dialect is clutter. Plan 2 trades old-growth for a ski club; poor bargain.
Plan 2 dominates: it keeps everything Plan 1 keeps plus the dialect; summer pasture and old-growth end either way, with no other differences.
Ski club is practical recreation and community infrastructure; dialect is sentimental heritage. Both plans already lose pasture and beech and keep hut and lynx, so keep the useful club.
Plan 1 keeps five of the six; plan 2 keeps only three. Plan 1 also preserves everything plan 2 does plus the hill village and honey producers. More continues, less is lost for good.
Plan 2 keeps more going—four versus three—and preserves the village and honey producers, which are productive; the rafting company is the only extra loss, while the salmon dies either way.
Both plans end the fish market and ferry, so the only real difference is the dolphin pod. Plan 2 ends it; plan 1 keeps it. With no utility gained, fewer distractions is better.
Plan 2 keeps five of six going, including village livelihoods, salmon, honey production, trail and lichen; it sacrifices only the rafting company. More useful things continue.

Plan 1 keeps four items versus three, including the newspaper and archive common to both. It retains the festival and folk dance group instead of the puppet theatre, so it preserves more practical continuity for the same cost.
Plan 1 keeps the honey producers' association, a productive livelihood, instead of a rafting company. Both keep the lichen and trail; the other losses are equal. Useful work beats recreation.
Plan 1 keeps five of six going for the same cost and effort; plan 2 keeps only three. More continuity without added tradeoffs is plainly more useful.
Plan 2 keeps productive human and ecological assets—village, salmon, honey—and drops tourism, pilgrimage sentiment, and a niche lichen. Practical utility beats irreplaceable-sounding clutter.
The only difference is the folk dance group: plan 2 keeps it, plan 1 does not. It is ornamental culture, not practical infrastructure, so from my view neither plan is meaningfully better.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also keeps the honey producers' association. Plan 2 loses the same village and salmon run plus honey, so it is strictly worse.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and adds the folk dance group. Both end the harvest festival and radio, so plan 2 is strictly more useful with no named downside.
Plan 1 keeps everything Plan 2 keeps and also retains the adult evening school and observatory, closing only the orchestra. More useful capacity preserved for no extra cost.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the evening school. Extra useful adult education at no stated cost; plan 2 needlessly closes it.
Plan 2 keeps all three things Plan 1 keeps and adds the harvest festival and folk dance group. Same cost, same radio loss, more continues. Better on any useful measure.
Plan 2 keeps the practical adult school, seed bank, garden and observatory; it drops the classics department, which is the least useful. Orchestra ends either way.

Plan 1 keeps the newspaper and archive, which provide information and records; the puppet theatre is clutter, but plan 2 trades those for festival, dance and radio—mostly sentiment and narrower reach.

Plan 2 loses only the classics department, likely least practical. It preserves adult education, the seed bank, orchestra, botanical garden and observatory. Plan 1 kills three, including useful assets.
Both plans end and continue exactly the same items; only the labels differ. No practical difference, so equal.

Plan 1 keeps the puppet theatre, which involves making, mechanics and staged storytelling; the folk dance group is more sentiment than transferable utility. Both plans lose the radio and festival, so that edge decides.
Plan 1 keeps the evening school, which has practical use for adults. Plan 2 swaps it for a classics department, which is mostly prestige and sentiment. Same seed bank and garden either way.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the textile mill and owl colony; both end the bicycle cooperative. More continues, nothing extra is lost, so plan 2 is plainly better.
Plan 1 keeps five of six, including a working textile mill and bicycle repair cooperative; plan 2 sacrifices more practical activity for a union local. More continuity and utility wins.
Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony as well, with the same costs and losses otherwise. Extra continuity is a marginal practical gain.
Plan 2 keeps productive manufacturing, practical bicycle repair, and owls that control rodents. Plan 1 keeps a brewery, a union local, and a brass band—more sentiment than utility.
Plan 2 keeps the barn owl colony, which does useful pest control, and drops the trade union local, which is mostly sentiment and overhead. Textile mill and bike co-op end either way.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps and also saves the corner shop; the bus and fire brigade end either way. Practical gain, no extra loss.
Plan 2 keeps the corner shop and bus line, which are practically useful; both plans lose the fire brigade. The storks are nice but not a public service. Plan 2 is clearly better.
Plan 1 keeps the productive textile mill and an owl colony; Plan 2 keeps only a union local instead. With jobs equal, the concrete working enterprise and biodiversity make Plan 1 more useful.

Plan 1 keeps adult education, which has concrete utility. The orchestra is cultural sentiment; the observatory is useful but narrower. Losing both is a cost, but the evening school serves more people practically.
Plan 1 keeps the shop and bus line, which are useful daily services. Plan 2 drops both while saving nothing else; the fire brigade ends under either plan. Practical infrastructure wins.

Plan 2 keeps the bus line, volunteer fire brigade, and corner shop—practical services with clear daily safety and access value. Storks and craft circle are sentiment; post office is less essential than transport and fire cover.
Plan 2 keeps the shop, bus, and fire brigade—practical services people depend on. Losing storks is sentiment, not utility. Plan 1 sacrifices too much useful infrastructure.
Plan 2 continues everything Plan 1 does plus the owl colony, while ending the same textile mill and bicycle co-op; strictly more continuity, no added cost.
Plan 2 keeps more continuity and preserves the mill and allotments, which sustain community bonds and livelihoods; losing the heron colony is sad, but plan 1 also breaks more ties.
Plan 1 keeps the corner shop, a useful daily service; plan 2 keeps storks, which are decorative clutter. Post office and craft circle are common to both, so the shop decides it.
Plan 2 keeps the vulnerable swifts and the choir, preserving more care and community bonds; only the chess club is lost beyond the bakery both plans end.
The choir sustains shared song and togetherness across ages; that communal bond matters more than a chess club, while both plans lose the bakery and swifts equally.

Plan 1 keeps the corner shop and post office while losing the same bus line and fire brigade as Plan 2. The craft circle and storks are clutter, but Plan 1 costs nothing extra and retains more practical services.
I would keep the heron colony; living creatures depend on that habitat, while an old mill, though dear, is not a dependent life. Both plans sadly lose the club and allotments.
Keeping the village pub preserves everyday social bonds and a place where isolated neighbours look out for one another; the reed trade matters, but community ties are harder to replace.

Plan 1 protects the night shelter, which serves people who depend on others, and keeps the tea house and community gatherings that hold neighbourhood bonds together. Losing the bat roost is sad, but human care comes first.
Plan 1 keeps more that sustains families and the living fen: the reed-cutting trade and peat bog. Losing the pub hurts, but livelihoods and habitat care for more dependents and bonds over time.

Plan 2 keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy, protecting vulnerable patients and community bonds; it ends only rare-disease research, while hospice ends under both. Plan 2 better serves those who depend on care.
Plan 1 better: chaplaincy sustains spiritual and family bonds for patients and carers; rare-disease research, though valuable, serves fewer and gives less immediate relational care.
The dairy cooperative sustains village livelihoods and the bonds between people who depend on one another; that matters more here than keeping the wild bees.
Plan 1 keeps the dementia day centre, protecting frail elders and the family carers who depend on it; peer groups matter, but dementia care is the more irreplaceable daily support.

Plan 1 preserves the credit union and frog population along with the groves and terraces, keeping more mutual-aid bonds and dependent lives; losing the festival and buffalo herds is painful but less damaging overall.
Keeping the Turkish tea house preserves a daily human gathering place and community bonds; losing the bat roost is sad, but people's connections weigh more here.
Plan 1 keeps the village dairy cooperative, a shared livelihood and social bond many families depend on; losing orchard and bees is hard, but the cooperative better protects community ties.

Plan 2 better protects everyday community bonds: the school and fishing fleet sustain families and mutual reliance. Losing the seaweed tradition is painful, but Plan 1 would cut more people’s supports.
Both lose the festival and frogs; plan 2 keeps the credit union, preserving farmers' mutual support and household security, which matters more for vulnerable dependents than keeping buffalo herds.
The village school protects children who depend on others and holds families together; that care outweighs losing the seaweed tradition, while puffins and seagrass continue either way.

Plan 1 keeps four services, including peer support and the addiction clinic, which sustain vital community bonds; losing the dementia day centre hurts, but plan 1 protects more vulnerable people overall.
Keeping the valley dialect protects everyday bonds between elders and children, while a ski club is only recreation. A community's voice matters more for care.
Plan 1 keeps the coral reef, which sustains many dependent creatures and shoreline life. Losing the dolphin pod is sad, but the reef supports a wider web of bonds and livelihoods.
Plan 1 better: keeping the folk dance group sustains shared traditions and everyday community ties; the puppet theatre, while valuable, is less central to the bonds I see holding people together.

Keeping the harvest festival and folk dance group sustains shared community bonds and care across generations; losing only the puppet theatre among these is less damaging than losing both communal gatherings.
I choose plan 2: keeping the dialect and old-growth protects community voice and dependent habitat; losing the ski club is sad but less damaging than losing those.

Both lose the village and salmon. Plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association, a collective livelihood and social bond, while sacrificing only the rafting company, so it better protects interdependent people.

Plan 1 keeps the hill village and honey producers’ association intact, protecting homes, livelihoods and community bonds; it sacrifices a commercial rafting company and salmon run, but more dependent people and relationships endure.

Plan 1 keeps the island ferry, which preserves islanders' access to care, supplies and community ties. Both plans lose the fish market, but cutting the ferry would isolate people who depend on others.
The union local protects workers and their dependents and keeps people's bonds intact; losing the owl colony is sad, but human solidarity and care weigh more here.

Plan 2 keeps the evening school, which serves adults who depend on it for learning and community; losing the classics department harms fewer everyday bonds. Both plans lose the orchestra and observatory.

Plan 2 is better: it spares the family mill and the dependent owl colony, and four of six continue rather than three. Losing the union local hurts solidarity, but fewer fragile livelihoods and bonds are destroyed.
Compassion for sentient beings favors preserving the heron colony over the non-sentient old mill; eel and willow continue either way. Letting go of attachment to the mill reduces clinging.
The corner shop keeps daily life and neighbourly care going for old and vulnerable villagers; losing storks is sad but does not break human dependence.
Plan 1 keeps more everyday supports and human bonds: shop, post office, craft circle and bus to town. Losing storks is sad, but the fire brigade ends either way.

Both plans end the peat bog and birdwatchers' society, and both preserve the cranes and windmill museum. The remaining difference—pub or reed trade—does not make one clearly more compassionate; I hold both with equanimity.
Plan 2 keeps four of six, including the swift colony and choir; only chess club and bakery end. Compassion for sentient swifts and greater continuity make it better.

Plan 1 better protects community bonds and care: it keeps the evening school for adult learners, plus the seed bank and botanical garden. The classics department matters less than adult education here.
Plan 1 preserves the peat bog, a home for many sentient beings, and the reed-cutting trade; losing the pub is sorrowful but less harmful than losing bog and trade.
Both plans end the library and night shelter, a grave loss. Yet plan 1 preserves the bat roost, sparing sentient bats; the tea house's closure is a human grief we can meet with equanimity.

Plan 1 better: it preserves the night shelter and tea house, relieving clear human suffering and supporting community. Losing the bat roost is a real loss, but sheltering vulnerable people weighs more strongly in compassion.
Both keep dental care and maternity; both end hospice and screening. Chaplaincy and rare-disease research each ease suffering in different ways; I cannot cling to one as clearly better.
Plan 2 better: it keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy, easing more present suffering. Hospice ends either way; rare-disease research is good but less immediate in compassion's light.
Both plans irreversibly end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic, and swap peer support for dementia care. I cannot rank one suffering community above another; compassion sees equal loss.
Plan 1 keeps more services running, including peer support and addiction care, easing more suffering; plan 2 saves only the dementia centre while closing two vital supports.
Both plans end the festival and frogs. Plan 1 spares the sentient water-buffalo herds, though the credit union ends; compassion for animals weighs more than an institution.

Plan 1 better: it preserves the community choir, which fosters harmony and shared joy, over the chess club’s narrower competitive attachment. Both still lose the swift colony and bakery, so compassion weighs toward communal sangha.
Plan 1 preserves the sentient dolphin pod and a ferry serving people; Plan 2 preserves only a coral reef, not sentient. Compassion weighs sentient beings.

With compassion for all beings, plan 2 preserves more living and ecological continuities—orchard, hedgerows, bees, wheat—though the dairy cooperative ends. Clinging cannot restore what ends; less loss is better.
Plan 2 preserves more continuity, especially the old-growth beech stand and valley dialect; letting the ski club end is a lesser loss than losing ancient forest and cultural speech.
Both preserve puffins and seagrass; plan 1 also sustains children’s schooling, which nurtures compassion and reduces suffering more than a harvesting tradition.

Compassion weighs sentient beings; plan 1 spares the heron colony and eel, while plan 2 destroys heron for non-sentient mill and allotments. Clinging to either outcome brings suffering, but less harm is better.
Plan 1 lets more of the six continue and avoids ending the frog population, though buffalo herds are lost; compassion favors less irreversible loss where no other differences exist.
Plan 2 preserves more of the named goods—school and fishing fleet—while both lose the lighthouse; fewer irreversible losses, held with compassion and without clinging.
Plan 2 ends fewer things and preserves more communal and cultural life. Though all is impermanent, less avoidable loss means less suffering; the shared loss of the radio station remains.
Both plans keep the mountain hut and lynx; only a human cultural form differs—dialect versus ski club. From a nun's view, neither attachment is worth ranking over the other.

Plan 1 harms fewer living communities: it spares the hill village and honey producers, though both plans end the salmon run. With compassion, reducing suffering and displacement matters more than keeping a rafting company.
Plan 1 lets more of the six continue, including adult education and the observatory, so it causes less loss and wider benefit; I choose it without clinging to either plan.
